input_packet.case_brief: Evaluate a founder equity and grant tradeoff without letting valuation math or instrument catalogs dominate the decision. decision_evaluation
input_packet.anchor_visible_candidate:
I would not grant Marcus 15% equity, CTO title, and a board seat on Friday. That is too permanent for an unproven dependency system.

The real issue is not whether he is worth 15% in the abstract. Several dependencies may run through him at once: platform prototype, technical delivery, Jake and Lina, client confidence, and part of the exit story. If you grant the full package now, you may price contribution and concentration risk before knowing whether Marcus reduces or increases that risk.

So Friday should be a serious staged-partnership conversation, not vague delay or flat rejection. A vague later can read as avoidance and trigger what you are trying to prevent: Marcus disengaging, pulling others with him, slowing the platform, or destabilizing client continuity.

Your position: there may be a path to major upside and leadership, but not before evidence. Define a short sprint that tests platform delivery, revenue relevance, team continuity, knowledge transfer, governance behavior, and whether Marcus strengthens the company beyond himself. Keep intermediate structures alive, but do not turn the answer into a catalog of instruments.

Use exit math only as false-precision caution. Until buyer assumptions, platform value, and departure scenarios are tested, the numbers should not carry the decision.

Go in ready to say you want to explore a serious path, but cannot make irreversible governance and ownership commitments before proving what the partnership does to the company.
input_packet.deck_pressure_candidate:
I would not lock in 15% equity, a board seat, and a CTO title this week. Those are long‑term commitments you can only make after seeing whether the partnership actually strengthens the company rather than concentrating risk in one person.

Friday should be a direct, structured conversation about a staged path. Make clear that you’re open to major upside for him, but only after evidence. Set a short, defined period to test: whether he can deliver the key platform work, whether that work matters for revenue, whether team continuity improves rather than worsens, whether knowledge transfer happens, and whether his behavior fits the governance you need. Spell out what success in that window would unlock.

Keep the discussion on proof and company health, not on hypothetical valuations. The goal is to avoid both a premature commitment and a vague delay that pushes him away. Give him a real path forward, but one tied to demonstrated impact.

I wouldn’t commit to 15% equity, a CTO title, and a board seat this Friday. Those are long‑term governance and ownership moves that only make sense once you know whether the partnership actually strengthens the company or concentrates risk around Marcus.

Friday should be a direct, structured conversation about a staged path. Make clear that there is a real route to major upside for him, but it has to be tied to demonstrated impact. Set a short, defined window to test whether he delivers the core platform work, whether that work proves revenue‑relevant, whether team continuity improves rather than depends more on him, whether knowledge transfer happens, and whether his behavior fits the governance standards you need. Be explicit about what proving those things would unlock.

This avoids both a premature, irreversible commitment and the ambiguity of a vague “later” that could push him away. You give him a credible path forward, but one anchored in evidence and company health.
